fields.title: Job
fields.subtitle: Iyov, “The Book of Job”
fields.description: The Bible’s great book about suffering, which asks its question in the first chapter: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” A blameless man in the land of Uz loses his wealth, his children and his health in a few days, and says, “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away.” Then three friends sit with him in silence for seven days, and then argue, chapter after chapter, that he must have sinned, while Job curses the day he was born, demands a hearing from God, and rises to the words “I know that my Redeemer lives.” A poem asking where wisdom can be found; a young man named Elihu; and at last the LORD answering Job from the storm: “Where were you when I founded the earth?” Set out line by line as the poetry it is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Job about?
qa.answer: A righteous man who loses everything and wrestles with God over why. In the prose prologue (chapters 1–2) the Accuser in the heavenly court claims that Job serves God only for what he gets, and God allows him to be tested: Job loses his wealth, his ten children and his health, but does not curse God. In the long poetic middle (3:1–42:6) his three friends insist that he must be suffering for his sins, Job protests his innocence and demands that God answer him, a young man named Elihu speaks, and finally the LORD answers Job from the storm. In the prose epilogue God rebukes the friends, says that Job has spoken rightly of him, and restores Job’s fortunes.

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Job, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author or say when it was written. One ancient Jewish tradition credited it to Moses. The story is set in a patriarchal world outside Israel, in the land of Uz, where Job offers sacrifices for his own family and counts his wealth in flocks and herds, but that tells us when the story is set rather than when the book was written. Scholars have proposed dates from the time of Solomon to after the exile, and the question remains open. Ezekiel 14:14 names Job with Noah and Daniel, and James 5:11 speaks of Job’s endurance.

qa.question: Who is the Accuser in the book of Job?
qa.answer: In chapters 1–2 a figure called in Hebrew “the satan”, with the article, comes among the heavenly beings before the LORD and questions Job’s motives: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” The word is a title meaning the adversary or accuser, which this translation renders “the Accuser”. Later Scripture uses the word as a name, Satan, for God’s great enemy, and many Christians identify him with this figure. The book of Job itself presents him as an accuser in the heavenly court who can act only as far as the LORD allows, and he disappears from the story after chapter 2.

qa.question: What does “I know that my Redeemer lives” mean in Job?
qa.answer: In Job 19:25–27, abandoned by his family and friends, Job declares that his Redeemer lives and will stand up for him at the last, and that he will see God for himself. The Redeemer, in Hebrew go’el, was the nearest relative who stood up for a family member in trouble, buying back his land, freeing him from slavery and defending him in court. Most interpreters think Job means God himself, who will in the end take his side. Christians have long heard in the words a hope fulfilled in Christ and in the resurrection of the body; Handel set them at the opening of the third part of Messiah.

qa.question: Does God ever explain to Job why he suffered?
qa.answer: No. When the LORD answers Job from the storm (chapters 38–41), he never mentions the scene in heaven or gives a reason for Job’s suffering. Instead he asks Job a long series of questions about the making of the world and the wild creatures he cares for, from the stars to the raven, and shows him Behemoth and Leviathan. Job is answered all the same: “I had heard of you by what my ears were told, but now my own eyes have seen you.” The book does not solve the problem of suffering. It shows a man who meets God in the middle of it, and God declares that Job, who argued honestly with him, spoke rightly, while the friends who defended him with false reasons did not.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The poetry, which runs from chapter 3 to 42:6, is printed one line at a time, and “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
The Accuser answered the LORD, “Does Job fear God for nothing?”

— Job 1:9

Everyone has heard of Job. His patience is a proverb, and his name has become shorthand for anyone who suffers much and complains little. But people who actually read the book are often surprised. The Job of chapters 1 and 2 is patient indeed. The Job of the next forty chapters curses the day he was born, accuses God of hunting him down, demands his day in court, and tells his friends that they are “miserable comforters”. And at the end of the book, God says that Job, not his pious friends, has spoken rightly of him.

Job is the Bible’s great book about suffering, but it is not a book that explains suffering. It is a book about what happens to faith when suffering cannot be explained: whether a person can go on trusting God, and arguing with him, and still be his servant. Its question is asked in the first chapter, by the Accuser in the court of heaven: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” Is faith only a bargain that lasts as long as God keeps his side of it, or is God worth trusting for his own sake?

A man in the land of Uz

The story is set far from Israel, in “the land of Uz”, probably in Edom or the desert east of the Jordan, and in a world that feels very old. Job counts his wealth in flocks and herds, offers sacrifices for his family himself, as the patriarchs did, and lives to a great age. He is not an Israelite, and the book never mentions the exodus, the law of Moses or the temple. It is a story about a human being before God, and it speaks to anyone.

The book does not name its author or its date. One ancient Jewish tradition credited it to Moses; scholars have proposed dates from the time of Solomon to after the exile, and the question cannot be settled. The prophet Ezekiel names Job with Noah and Daniel as a byword for righteousness (Ezekiel 14:14), and James in the New Testament speaks of “Job’s endurance” and of the outcome the Lord gave (James 5:11). Its Hebrew is among the most difficult in the Old Testament, rich in rare words, and its poetry among the greatest ever written.

The shape of the book

Job is built like a great arch, with a prose story at either end and poetry in between:

  • The prologue (chapters 1–2), in prose: Job’s goodness, the two scenes in heaven, his losses, and his friends’ arrival.
  • Job’s lament (chapter 3), in which he curses the day of his birth.
  • The debate (chapters 4–27): three rounds of speeches, in which each of Job’s friends speaks in turn, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, and Job answers each one. The rounds grow shorter as the friends run out of things to say; in the third, Bildad’s speech is only six verses long and Zophar does not speak at all.
  • A poem on wisdom (chapter 28).
  • Job’s final defence (chapters 29–31), ending, “The words of Job are ended.”
  • The speeches of Elihu (chapters 32–37), a young man who has been listening.
  • The LORD’s speeches from the storm (38:1–42:6), with Job’s two brief replies.
  • The epilogue (42:7–17), in prose: the friends rebuked, Job restored.

The question in heaven

The book opens on a man who is “blameless and upright; he feared God and turned away from evil.” He has seven sons and three daughters and great wealth, and he is so careful that after his children’s feasts he offers sacrifices for them, in case they have “sinned and cursed God in their hearts.”

Then the scene moves to heaven, where “the sons of God”, members of God’s council, present themselves before the LORD, and among them is the Accuser. It is the LORD who raises Job’s name: “Have you considered my servant Job?” The Accuser answers with the question that drives the book. Of course Job is good, he says; God has put “a protective hedge around him”. Take away what he has, “and he will surely curse you to your face.”

The LORD allows the test, within limits: “Only do not lay a hand on the man himself.” In a single day Job loses everything. Four messengers come, each arriving before the last has finished, each with the same terrible refrain: “I am the only one who has escaped to tell you.” His oxen, donkeys, sheep and camels are gone, his servants killed, and all ten of his children crushed when a great wind brings down the house where they are eating. Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground, and worships:

He said, “I came naked from my mother’s womb, and naked I will go back there. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; may the name of the LORD be blessed.”

— Job 1:21

A second test takes his health. He sits among the ashes, scraping his sores with a piece of broken pottery, and his wife says what the Accuser had predicted: “Curse God and die!” Job answers, “Are we to accept good from God and not accept trouble as well?”

Everything that follows depends on one fact: the reader knows what Job never learns. We have seen the scene in heaven. We know that Job is not being punished, that the LORD himself has called him blameless, and that he suffers, as the LORD says, “for no reason”. Job and his friends know none of this. They must make sense of his suffering from below, and that is exactly what they cannot do.

Seven days of silence

Three friends hear of Job’s troubles and come to comfort him. When they see him, they do not recognise him. They weep, tear their robes, and sit with him on the ground for seven days and nights: “No one said a word to him, because they saw how great his suffering was.” It is the best thing they do in the whole book. Readers who have sat with the grieving know why.

Then Job speaks, and what he says is not patient at all. He curses the day he was born: “Let the day I was born perish”. He asks why he did not die at birth, why light is given to those in misery. It is one of the darkest chapters in Scripture, and it is in Scripture. The Bible does not ask the suffering to pretend.

The friends’ answer

The friends are not fools, and they are not villains. They are devout men who believe, with most people in every age, that the world is morally ordered: God rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked. Eliphaz appeals to experience and to a vision in the night: “Think back now: who that was innocent has ever perished?” Bildad appeals to the wisdom of tradition: “Does God twist justice?” Zophar is blunter still, and tells Job that God has overlooked part of his guilt.

Much of what they say is true in general, and some of it is quoted elsewhere in the Bible. Eliphaz’s “How blessed is the one whom God corrects!” could stand in Proverbs. But applied to Job, it is false, and the reader knows it. As the debate goes on, the friends grow harsher. Since Job suffers, he must have sinned; since he will not confess, he must be proud as well. By the third round Eliphaz is listing the sins Job must have committed. Their theology has no room for an innocent sufferer, so they must make Job guilty to keep it.

Job’s replies are sometimes bitter: “No doubt you are the people who matter, and wisdom will die with you!” He calls them “worthless physicians”, and says their greatest wisdom would be silence. But his real argument is not with them. It is with God.

From despair to hope

Job does not doubt that God exists or that God is in control. That is precisely his problem. He believes, as the friends do, that God governs everything, and so he can only conclude that God has turned against him. He wants to take God to court, but how can a mortal argue his case with God?

For he is not a human being like me, that I could answer him, that we could go to court together. There is no one to judge between us, who could lay his hand on us both.

— Job 9:32–33

And yet, in the middle of his protests, flashes of hope break through, each a little brighter than the last. He will trust God even if God kills him:

Even if he kills me, I will hope in him; still, I will defend my ways to his face.

— Job 13:15

He asks, “If a mortal dies, will they live again?” He senses that somewhere there must be one who will take his side:

Even now my witness is in heaven; the one who vouches for me is on high.

— Job 16:19

And in chapter 19, abandoned by his family, mocked by children, having “escaped with only the skin of my teeth”, he rises to the most famous words in the book:

But I know that my Redeemer lives, and that at the last he will stand upon the dust. And after my skin has been destroyed like this, yet in my flesh I will see God, whom I myself will see on my side, whom my own eyes will behold, and not as a stranger. My heart faints within me!

— Job 19:25–27

The Redeemer, in Hebrew go’el, was the nearest relative, whose duty was to stand up for a family member in trouble: to buy back his land, free him from slavery, and defend him in court. Job’s relatives have deserted him, yet he is sure that his Redeemer lives and will stand up for him at the last. Most interpreters think he means God himself: the God who seems to be his enemy will in the end be on his side. Christians have long heard in these words, set to music in Handel’s Messiah, a hope that only the resurrection of Christ fulfils. Whatever Job himself saw, he saw further than anyone around him.

Where can wisdom be found?

Chapter 28 is a quiet interlude, a poem that may be spoken by Job or by the narrator. It describes miners tunnelling deep into the earth for silver, gold and precious stones, going where no bird of prey has looked. Human beings can find almost anything. But then it asks:

But where can wisdom be found? Where is the place of understanding?

— Job 28:12

Wisdom cannot be dug up or bought. Only God knows where it is, and the poem ends with his word to humanity:

And he said to humankind, “Look, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding.”

— Job 28:28

It is exactly how the book first described Job: a man who “feared God and turned away from evil.” The poem tells us that, whatever his friends say, Job has lived the wise life all along.

Job’s last words

In chapters 29–31 Job makes his final defence. He remembers the days “when God watched over me”, when he was honoured at the city gate because “I was eyes for the blind and feet for the lame.” He describes his present humiliation. And then he swears a long oath of innocence, listing sins he has not committed, beginning with “I made a covenant with my eyes”, and calling down curses on himself if he is lying. He signs it, as it were, and waits: “Here is my signature; let the Almighty answer me!”

Elihu

The answer does not come at once. Instead a young man named Elihu, who has held back out of respect for his elders, bursts in, angry with Job “because Job made himself out to be in the right rather than God”, and angry with the friends for finding no answer. For six chapters he speaks. He adds an important thought the friends had not: that God may use suffering not only to punish but to teach, that “He rescues the afflicted through their suffering and opens their ears through distress.” As he speaks, a storm seems to gather, and he ends with God’s majesty.

Readers have disagreed about Elihu. Some see him as a brash young man who repeats the friends’ errors at greater length; others see him as preparing the way for God, and value his insight into suffering as discipline. Neither Job nor God answers him, and the epilogue does not mention him.

The LORD answers from the storm

At last “the LORD answered Job from the storm”. Job had asked for a hearing, and he gets one. But God does not answer Job’s questions. He asks his own:

Who is this who makes my plan obscure with words that lack knowledge? Brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you will tell me the answers. Where were you when I founded the earth? Tell me, if you have such understanding.

— Job 38:2–4

What follows is a tour of creation unlike anything else in Scripture: the foundations of the earth, laid “while the morning stars were singing together”, the sea shut in behind doors, the dawn given its orders, the storerooms of the snow, the stars of the Pleiades and Orion. Then the animals: the lioness and the raven, the mountain goat, the wild donkey, the wild ox, the ostrich, the war horse, the hawk. Most of them are wild creatures, useless to human beings and beyond their control, and God cares for every one.

Job is silenced: “I am so small; how can I answer you? I put my hand over my mouth.” But God speaks again, and asks, “Would you condemn me to prove that you are right?” He shows Job two great creatures, Behemoth and Leviathan, beasts of overwhelming power that no human can tame, and that God made and rules. “Everything under the whole heaven is mine.”

God never tells Job about the scene in heaven. He never explains why Job suffered. Yet Job is answered. He has met God, and that is enough:

I had heard of you by what my ears were told, but now my own eyes have seen you. So I take back what I said, and I repent in dust and ashes.

— Job 42:5–6

The ending

The prose epilogue brings a surprise. The LORD is angry with Eliphaz and his two friends, “because you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.” The men who defended God are rebuked; the man who argued with him is vindicated. Honest protest addressed to God is better than pious falsehood spoken about him. The friends must bring sacrifices, and Job must pray for them. “When Job prayed for his friends, the LORD restored his fortunes”.

Job receives twice the flocks and herds he had before, and seven sons and three daughters. The daughters are named, Jemimah, Keziah and Keren-happuch, are said to be the most beautiful in the land, and receive an inheritance with their brothers, which was unusual. Some readers find the happy ending too neat, as if it undid the book’s hard lessons. But it does not say that Job’s faith was a bargain after all; the test is over, and his faith had held when he had nothing. And it does not pretend that his first children are replaced. Some interpreters have noticed that the animals are doubled but the children are not, and suggested that his first ten were not lost to him for ever. Job dies “old and satisfied with his days.”

How to read Job

Job is long, and much of it is argument, so it helps to know the shape before you begin. Read the prologue and the epilogue first, to see the frame, and then read the poetry in large portions, a whole speech at a time, listening for how each speaker answers the last. Do not treat every sentence as Scripture’s last word on its subject: the friends say many things that God later calls wrong. The book is a debate, and its meaning comes from the whole, not from any one speech.

If you are suffering, you may find you need Job’s laments more than its answers. They are there to be prayed. If you are trying to help someone who suffers, take the friends’ seven days of silence as your model, and their speeches as a warning.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices are worth knowing before you begin.

Poetry, line by line. Almost all of Job, from chapter 3 to 42:6, is poetry, and this edition prints each line on its own, as the Hebrew sets it out, so that you can hear the parallel lines answering one another.

“The Accuser.” The figure in the heavenly court is called in Hebrew the satan, with the article, a title meaning the adversary or accuser rather than a personal name. This translation renders it “the Accuser”. Many readers identify him with Satan, God’s great enemy, as later Scripture names him; the book of Job itself presents him as the accuser who can act only as far as the LORD allows.

“The Almighty.” Job’s favourite name for God is Shaddai, one of the oldest names of God, which appears more often in Job than in any other book. It is translated “the Almighty”.

“Curse.” In 1:5, 1:11, 2:5 and 2:9 the Hebrew uses the word “bless” where it means “curse”, out of reverence, rather than write that anyone cursed God. The translation gives the meaning.

“I take back what I said.” The Hebrew of Job’s last words (42:6) is brief and has been read in several ways. The translation takes Job to be withdrawing what he said without knowledge, not confessing the hidden sins his friends had charged him with, since the LORD at once declares that Job has spoken rightly.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Job 1
fields.body_html:
Job, a blameless man in the land of Uz

There was a man in the land of Uz named Job. He was blameless and upright; he feared God and turned away from evil. He had seven sons and three daughters. He owned 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen and 500 female donkeys, and he had a great many servants. He was the greatest man among all the peoples of the East. His sons used to take turns holding a feast, each in his own house on his day, and they would send for their three sisters and invite them to eat and drink with them. Whenever a round of feasting was over, Job would send for his children and consecrate them. He would get up early in the morning and offer a burnt offering for each one of them, because Job said to himself, “Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts.” This is what Job always did.

Does Job fear God for nothing?

One day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and the Accuser also came among them.
The LORD said to the Accuser, “Where have you come from?” The Accuser answered the LORD, “From roaming the earth and walking up and down on it.”
The LORD said to the Accuser, “Have you considered my servant Job? There is no one like him on earth: a man blameless and upright, who fears God and turns away from evil.”
The Accuser answered the LORD, “Does Job fear God for nothing?”
Have you not put a protective hedge around him and his household and everything he owns on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his flocks and herds have spread throughout the land.
But stretch out your hand and strike everything he has, and he will surely curse you to your face.
The LORD said to the Accuser, “Very well, everything he has is in your power. Only do not lay a hand on the man himself.” Then the Accuser went out from the presence of the LORD.
One day Job’s sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their oldest brother.
A messenger came to Job and said, “The oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing beside them,
when the Sabeans swept down and carried them off. They killed the servants with the sword, and I am the only one who has escaped to tell you.”
While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, “The fire of God fell from the sky and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them. I am the only one who has escaped to tell you.”
While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, “The Chaldeans formed three raiding parties, swept down on the camels and carried them off. They killed the servants with the sword, and I am the only one who has escaped to tell you.”
While he was still speaking, another messenger came and said, “Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their oldest brother,
when suddenly a great wind came from across the desert and struck the four corners of the house. It fell on the young people, and they are dead. I am the only one who has escaped to tell you.”
Then Job got up, tore his robe and shaved his head. He fell to the ground and worshiped.
He said, “I came naked from my mother’s womb,
and naked I will go back there.
The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away;
may the name of the LORD be blessed.”
In all this Job did not sin or accuse God of wrongdoing.

fields.title: Job 2
fields.body_html:
Job is struck in his own body

On another day the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and the Accuser also came among them to present himself before the LORD. The LORD said to the Accuser, “Where have you come from?” The Accuser answered the LORD, “From roaming the earth and walking up and down on it.” The LORD said to the Accuser, “Have you considered my servant Job? There is no one like him on earth: a man blameless and upright, who fears God and turns away from evil. He still holds firmly to his integrity, even though you stirred me up against him to destroy him for no reason.” The Accuser answered the LORD, “Skin for skin! People will give everything they have to save their own lives. But stretch out your hand and strike his bone and his flesh, and he will surely curse you to your face.” The LORD said to the Accuser, “Very well, he is in your power. Only spare his life.” So the Accuser went out from the presence of the LORD and struck Job with painful sores from the soles of his feet to the top of his head. Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself with as he sat among the ashes. His wife said to him, “Are you still holding on to your integrity? Curse God and die!” He said to her, “You are talking like one of the foolish women. Are we to accept good from God and not accept trouble as well?” In all this Job did not sin in what he said.

Three friends come to comfort Job

When Job’s three friends, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite, heard about all the trouble that had come on him, they set out, each from his own home. They had agreed to meet and go together to show him sympathy and comfort him. When they saw him from a distance, they did not recognize him. They wept aloud, and each of them tore his robe, and they threw dust into the air onto their heads. Then they sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him, because they saw how great his suffering was.

fields.title: Job 3
fields.body_html:
Job curses the day he was born

After this Job opened his mouth and cursed the day he was born.

And Job spoke up and said:
Let the day I was born perish,
and the night that said, ‘A boy has been conceived!’
That day, let it be darkness!
May God above not look for it,
and may no daylight shine on it.
May darkness and deep gloom claim it as their own;
may a cloud settle over it;
may all that blackens the day terrify it.
That night, let thick darkness carry it off;
let it not rejoice among the days of the year
or come into the count of the months.
Yes, let that night be barren;
let no cry of joy be heard in it.
Let those who lay curses on days curse it,
those who are skilled to rouse Leviathan.
Let the stars of its early dawn be dark;
let it wait for light that never comes
and never see the dawn open its eyes.
For it did not shut the doors of my mother’s womb
or hide trouble from my eyes.
Why did I not die at birth,
come out of the womb and breathe my last?
Why were there knees to receive me,
and breasts for me to nurse at?
For by now I would be lying at peace;
I would be asleep and at rest,
with the kings and counselors of the earth,
who rebuilt ruined places for themselves,
or with officials who had gold,
who filled their houses with silver.
Or why was I not like a stillborn child, hidden away,
like infants who never see the light?
There the wicked stop their raging,
and there those whose strength is spent are at rest.
Prisoners are at ease together;
they no longer hear the shout of the slave driver.
Small and great are there alike,
and slaves are free from their masters.
Why is light given to those in misery,
and life to the bitter in soul,
who long for death, but it does not come,
and search for it more than for hidden treasure,
who are filled with joy
and glad when they find the grave,
to a man whose way is hidden from him,
whom God has fenced in?
For sighing comes to me in place of food,
and my groans pour out like water.
For the thing I feared has come upon me,
and what I dreaded has happened to me.
I have no ease, no quiet, no rest;
only turmoil comes.

fields.title: Job 4
fields.body_html:
Eliphaz answers: who that was innocent ever perished?

Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
If someone dares to say a word to you, will you lose patience?
Yet who can keep from speaking?
Think how you have taught many
and strengthened hands that hung limp.
Your words have lifted up those who stumbled,
and you have made firm the knees that were giving way.
But now it has come to you, and you lose patience;
it strikes you, and you are terrified.
Is not your fear of God your confidence,
and the integrity of your ways your hope?
Think back now: who that was innocent has ever perished?
Where have the upright been wiped out?
As I have seen, those who plow evil
and sow trouble harvest the same.
At the breath of God they perish;
by the blast of his anger they are finished.
The lion may roar and the fierce lion growl,
but the teeth of the young lions are broken.
The strong lion dies for lack of prey,
and the lioness’s cubs are scattered.
A word was brought to me in secret;
my ear caught only a whisper of it.
amid troubled thoughts from visions in the night,
when deep sleep falls on people,
fear and trembling came upon me
and made all my bones shake.
Then a spirit glided past my face;
the hair on my body stood on end.
It stood still, but I could not make out what it looked like.
A form was before my eyes;
there was silence, and then I heard a voice:
Can a mortal be righteous before God?
Can anyone be pure before their Maker?
Even in his servants he puts no trust,
and he charges his angels with error,
how much more those who live in houses of clay,
whose foundation is in the dust,
who are crushed like a moth!
Between morning and evening they are shattered;
unnoticed, they perish forever.
Is not the cord of their tent pulled up?
They die, and without wisdom.

fields.title: Job 5
fields.body_html:
Eliphaz: no one will answer you

Call out, then; is there anyone who will answer you?
To which of the holy ones will you turn?
For resentment kills the fool,
and envy slays the simple.
I myself have seen a fool putting down roots,
but suddenly I declared his home cursed.
His children are far from safety;
they are crushed in the court at the gate,
with no one to rescue them.
The hungry eat up his harvest,
taking it even from among the thorns,
and a trap lies open for their wealth.
Hardship does not spring up from the dust,
and trouble does not sprout from the soil.
No, human beings are born to trouble,
as sparks fly upward.
But as for me, I would turn to God
and lay my case before God.
He does great things beyond understanding,
wonders that cannot be counted.
He gives rain to the earth
and sends water on the fields.
He sets the lowly on high,
and those who mourn are lifted to safety.
He thwarts the schemes of the crafty,
so that their hands achieve nothing.
He catches the wise in their own cunning,
and the schemes of the devious are swept away.
In the daytime they run into darkness,
and at noon they grope as if it were night.
But he saves the needy from the sword of their mouths
and from the grip of the powerful.
So the poor have hope,
and injustice shuts its mouth.
How blessed is the one whom God corrects!
So do not reject the discipline of the Almighty.
For he wounds, but he also binds up;
he strikes, but his hands heal.
He will rescue you from six troubles;
in seven, no harm will touch you.
In famine he will redeem you from death,
and in war from the power of the sword.
You will be sheltered from the lash of the tongue,
and you will not fear destruction when it comes.
You will laugh at destruction and hunger,
and you need not fear the wild animals of the earth.
For you will be in covenant with the stones of the field,
and the wild animals will be at peace with you.
You will know that your home is secure;
you will look over your property and find nothing missing.
You will know that your offspring will be many,
your descendants like the grass of the earth.
You will come to your grave in full vigor,
like sheaves gathered in at harvest time.
We have looked into all this, and it is true.
So hear it and know it for your own good.

fields.title: Job 6
fields.body_html:
Job: if only my anguish could be weighed

Then Job answered:
If only my anguish could be weighed
and all my calamity laid on the scales!
For now it would outweigh the sand of the seas;
that is why my words have been wild.
For the arrows of the Almighty are in me,
and my spirit drinks their poison;
the terrors of God are lined up against me.
Does a wild donkey bray when it has grass,
or an ox bellow over its feed?
Can tasteless food be eaten without salt,
or is there any flavor in the slime of purslane?
I refuse to touch them;
they are like food that makes me sick.
Oh, that my request would be granted,
that God would give me what I hope for:
that God would be willing to crush me,
to let loose his hand and cut me off!
Then I would still have this comfort,
and I would leap for joy in pain that does not let up:
that I have not denied the words of the Holy One.
What strength do I have, that I should keep waiting?
What future do I have, that I should be patient?
Is my strength the strength of stone?
Is my flesh made of bronze?
Is it not true that I have no help in myself,
and any hope of success has been driven from me?
Someone in despair should have faithful love from a friend,
even one who forsakes the fear of the Almighty.
My friends have been as undependable as a desert stream,
like streambeds that run dry,
which run dark with ice
and swell with melting snow.
When the heat comes, they fall silent;
in the hot season they vanish from their beds.
Caravans turn aside from their route;
they go up into the wasteland and perish.
The caravans of Tema look for the streams;
the traveling companies of Sheba hope to find them.
They are disappointed, because they had been so sure;
they arrive there and are dismayed.
So now you have become like that stream:
you see something terrible and are afraid.
Have I ever said, “Give me something,”
or, “Pay a bribe for me out of your wealth”?
Or, “Rescue me from the enemy’s hand;
ransom me from the grip of the ruthless”?
Teach me, and I will be quiet;
show me where I have gone wrong.
How forceful honest words can be!
But what does your arguing prove?
Do you mean to correct my words
and treat the words of someone in despair as wind?
You would even cast lots for an orphan
and haggle over the price of your friend.
But now, please look at me;
I will not lie to your face.
Think again, please; do not be unjust.
Think again: I am still in the right in this.
Is there anything wrong on my tongue?
Can my palate not tell what is ruinous?

fields.title: Job 7
fields.body_html:
My days have no hope

Do not mortals have hard service on earth,
and are their days not like the days of a hired worker?
Like a slave who longs for the shade,
and like a hired worker who waits for his pay,
so I have been given months of emptiness as my share,
and nights of misery have been assigned to me.
When I lie down I think, “When will I get up?”
But the night drags on,
and I toss and turn until dawn.
My body is covered with worms and crusts of dirt;
my skin scabs over and then oozes again.
My days go faster than a weaver’s shuttle;
they come to an end without hope.
Remember that my life is only a breath;
my eyes will never again see anything good.
The eye that sees me now will see me no more;
your eyes will look for me, but I will be gone.
As a cloud fades and is gone,
so whoever goes down to Sheol does not come up again.
He will never return to his home again,
and his place will know him no more.
So I will not keep silent;
I will speak out in the anguish of my spirit;
I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.
Am I the sea, or the monster of the deep,
that you put me under guard?
When I think, “My bed will comfort me,
my couch will ease my complaint,”
then you frighten me with dreams
and terrify me with visions,
so that I would choose to be strangled,
death rather than this body of mine.
I loathe my life; I would not live forever.
Let me alone, for my days are only a breath.
What are mortals, that you make so much of them,
that you pay them so much attention,
that you inspect them every morning
and test them every moment?
How long before you look away from me
and let me alone long enough to swallow my spit?
If I have sinned, what harm have I done to you,
watcher of humankind?
Why have you made me your target,
so that I have become a burden to myself?
Why do you not pardon my offense
and take away my guilt?
For soon I will lie down in the dust;
you will look for me, but I will be gone.

fields.title: Job 8
fields.body_html:
Bildad: does God twist justice?

Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
How long will you go on talking like this?
Your words are a blustering wind.
Does God twist justice?
Does the Almighty twist what is right?
If your children sinned against him,
he handed them over to the power of their own wrongdoing.
But if you will seek God earnestly
and plead with the Almighty for mercy,
if you are pure and upright,
then he will rise up for you at once
and restore your rightful home.
Though your beginning was small,
your future will be very great.
Ask the generation that went before,
and consider what their ancestors discovered.
For we were born only yesterday and know nothing;
our days on earth are a shadow.
Will they not teach you and tell you,
bringing out words from their understanding?
Can papyrus grow tall where there is no marsh?
Can reeds flourish without water?
While it is still in flower and not yet cut,
it withers sooner than any other plant.
Such is the end of all who forget God;
the hope of the godless will perish.
What they rely on snaps like a thread;
what they trust in is a spider’s web.
They lean on their house, but it will not stand;
they cling to it, but it will not hold.
They are like a lush plant in the sunshine,
sending out shoots all over the garden.
Their roots twine around a pile of rocks;
they look for a hold among the stones.
But when they are torn from their place,
it disowns them: “I never saw you.”
See, that is the joy of their way,
and from the soil others will spring up.
Surely God does not reject anyone who is blameless,
nor does he take evildoers by the hand.
He will yet fill your mouth with laughter
and your lips with shouts of joy.
Those who hate you will be clothed with shame,
and the tent of the wicked will be gone.

fields.title: Job 9
fields.body_html:
Job answers: how can a mortal be in the right with God?

Then Job answered:
Yes, I know that it is so;
but how can a mortal be in the right before God?
If someone wished to argue a case with him,
they could not answer him once in a thousand times.
He is wise in heart and mighty in strength;
who has ever defied him and come away unharmed?
He moves mountains before they know it,
and overturns them in his anger.
He shakes the earth out of its place,
and its pillars tremble.
He speaks to the sun, and it does not rise;
he puts the stars under seal.
By himself he stretched out the heavens,
and he treads on the waves of the sea.
He made the Bear and Orion, the Pleiades,
and the star clusters of the south.
He does great things too deep to search out,
and wonders too many to count.
If he passes by me, I do not see him;
if he moves on, I cannot perceive him.
If he snatches something away, who can stop him?
Who can say to him, “What are you doing?”
God does not hold back his anger;
the helpers of Rahab bowed down beneath him.
How then could I answer him,
or choose my words to argue with him?
Even if I were in the right, I could not answer him;
I would have to beg my judge for mercy.
If I called and he answered me,
I would not believe that he was listening to me.
He would crush me with a storm
and multiply my wounds for no reason.
He would not let me catch my breath,
but would fill me with bitterness.
If it is a matter of strength, look, he is the mighty one!
If it is a matter of justice, he says, “Who can summon me?”
Even if I were in the right, my own mouth would condemn me;
though I am blameless, it would prove me crooked.
I am blameless, yet I no longer care about myself;
I loathe my life.
It is all the same; that is why I say,
“He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.”
When a disaster brings sudden death,
he mocks at the despair of the innocent.
The earth is handed over to the wicked;
he blindfolds its judges.
If it is not he, then who is it?
My days go by faster than a runner;
they slip away without seeing anything good.
They glide past like boats made of reeds,
like an eagle swooping down on its prey.
If I say, “I will forget my complaint;
I will put away my sad face and smile,”
I am still afraid of all my pains,
for I know you will not declare me innocent.
I am going to be found guilty anyway;
why then should I struggle in vain?
Even if I washed myself with snow
and cleaned my hands with lye,
even then you would plunge me into a filthy pit,
so that my own clothes would loathe me.
For he is not a human being like me, that I could answer him,
that we could go to court together.
There is no one to judge between us,
who could lay his hand on us both.
Let him take his rod off me,
and let the dread of him no longer terrify me;
then I would speak without fear of him.
But as things are with me, I cannot.

fields.title: Job 10
fields.body_html:
I will speak in the bitterness of my soul

I am sick of my life;
I will give free rein to my complaint;
I will speak out of the bitterness of my soul.
I will say to God: Do not condemn me;
tell me what charges you have against me.
Does it please you to oppress me,
to reject the work of your own hands,
while you smile on the schemes of the wicked?
Do you have human eyes?
Do you see things as a mortal sees them?
Are your days like the days of a mortal,
or your years like a human lifetime,
that you must hunt for my guilt
and search out my sin,
although you know that I am not guilty,
and that no one can rescue me from your hand?
Your hands shaped me and made me;
and now you turn around and destroy me completely.
Remember that you molded me like clay;
will you now turn me back to dust?
Did you not pour me out like milk
and let me thicken like cheese?
You clothed me with skin and flesh
and knit me together with bones and sinews.
You gave me life and showed me faithful love,
and your care has watched over my spirit.
Yet all the while you hid this in your heart;
I know that this was your purpose.
If I sinned, you would be watching me
and would not let my guilt go unpunished.
If I am guilty, woe to me!
And if I am in the right, I still cannot lift up my head,
for I am filled with shame and see only my misery.
If I hold my head high, you hunt me like a lion
and again show your wondrous power against me.
You bring new witnesses against me
and increase your anger toward me;
you send wave after wave of troops against me.
Why did you bring me out of the womb?
I wish I had died before any eye had seen me.
I would be as if I had never existed,
carried straight from the womb to the grave.
Are not my days few? Then stop!
Leave me alone, so I can have a little cheer,
before I go to the place from which I will not return,
to the land of darkness and deep shadow,
a land of gloom as dark as night,
of deep shadow without any order,
where even the light is like darkness.

fields.title: Job 11
fields.body_html:
Zophar: God’s wisdom is beyond your reach

Then Zophar the Naamathite answered:
Should such a flood of words go unanswered?
Should a man be proved right by talking?
Should your empty talk reduce people to silence?
When you mock, should no one shame you?
For you say, ‘My teaching is sound,
and I am clean in your sight.’
But oh, if only God would speak,
and open his lips against you!
and show you the secrets of wisdom,
for true wisdom has two sides.
Know then that God has overlooked part of your guilt.
Can you discover the depths of God?
Can you reach the limits of the Almighty?
It is higher than the heavens; what can you do?
It is deeper than Sheol; what can you know?
Its measure is longer than the earth
and wider than the sea.
If he passes through and arrests someone
and calls the court together,
who can stop him?
For he knows who is false;
when he sees wickedness, will he not take note of it?
A senseless person will become wise
when a wild donkey’s colt is born human.
If you set your heart right
and spread out your hands to him,
if there is wrong in your hand, put it far away,
and let no injustice live in your tents,
then you will lift up your face without shame;
you will stand firm and have no fear.
You will forget your trouble;
you will remember it like water that has flowed away.
Your life will be brighter than noonday;
its darkness will become like the morning.
You will feel secure, because there is hope;
you will look around you and rest in safety.
You will lie down with no one to make you afraid,
and many will seek your favor.
But the eyes of the wicked will fail;
there will be no escape for them,
and their only hope will be to breathe their last.

fields.title: Job 12
fields.body_html:
Job answers: I am not inferior to you

Then Job answered:
No doubt you are the people who matter,
and wisdom will die with you!
But I have a mind as well as you;
I am not inferior to you.
Who does not know such things?
I have become a laughingstock to my friends,
I who called on God and he answered me;
a righteous and blameless man is laughed at!
Those at ease look with contempt on disaster;
they think it is ready for those whose feet are slipping.
The tents of robbers are at peace,
and those who provoke God are secure,
those who carry their god in their hands.
But ask the animals, and they will teach you;
ask the birds of the sky, and they will tell you.
Or speak to the earth, and it will teach you,
and the fish of the sea will declare it to you.
Which of all these does not know
that the hand of the LORD has done this?
In his hand is the life of every living creature
and the breath of every human being.
Does not the ear test words
as the tongue tastes food?
Wisdom is with the aged,
and long life brings understanding.
With God are wisdom and might;
counsel and understanding are his.
When he tears down, it cannot be rebuilt;
when he shuts someone in, no one can open it.
When he holds back the waters, they dry up;
when he lets them loose, they overwhelm the land.
With him are strength and true wisdom;
the misled and the misleader are both his.
He leads counselors away stripped
and makes fools of judges.
He loosens the bonds that kings put on others
and binds a captive’s cloth around their own waists.
He leads priests away stripped
and overthrows those firmly in power.
He silences trusted advisers
and takes away the judgment of elders.
He pours contempt on nobles
and loosens the belt of the mighty.
He reveals deep things from the darkness
and brings the deepest darkness into the light.
He makes nations great, then destroys them;
he enlarges nations, then leads them away.
He takes away the understanding of the leaders of the earth
and makes them wander in a trackless waste.
They grope in the dark without light,
and he makes them stagger like drunkards.

fields.title: Job 13
fields.body_html:
Job wants to argue his case with God

Look, my eyes have seen all this;
my ears have heard it and understood it.
What you know, I know too;
I am not inferior to you.
But I want to speak to the Almighty;
I long to argue my case with God.
But you smear things over with lies;
all of you are worthless physicians.
If only you would keep completely silent!
That would be wisdom on your part.
Please listen to my argument;
pay attention to the case I plead.
Will you speak what is unjust on God’s behalf,
and say what is false for him?
Will you show him partiality?
Will you plead the case for God?
Would it go well for you if he examined you?
Can you fool him as you would fool a mortal?
He will certainly rebuke you
if you secretly show partiality.
Will his majesty not fill you with terror?
Will the dread of him not fall on you?
Your wise sayings are proverbs made of ashes;
your defenses are defenses of clay.
Be quiet and leave me alone, so that I may speak;
then let come on me what may.
Why should I take my flesh in my teeth
and put my life in my hands?
Even if he kills me, I will hope in him;
still, I will defend my ways to his face.
This too will turn out for my deliverance,
since no godless person would come before him.
Listen closely to what I say;
let my declaration reach your ears.
See now, I have prepared my case;
I know that I will be vindicated.
Who is there that can bring a case against me?
If anyone can, I will be silent and die.
Only do not do two things to me,
and then I will not hide from your presence.
Take your hand away from me,
and do not let the terror of you frighten me.
Then call me, and I will answer;
or let me speak, and you answer me.
How many wrongs and sins have I committed?
Show me my offense and my sin.
Why do you hide your face
and treat me as your enemy?
Will you frighten a leaf blown by the wind?
Will you chase after dry straw?
For you write down bitter charges against me
and make me pay for the sins of my youth.
You put my feet in the stocks
and keep watch on all my paths;
you set a mark on the soles of my feet.
So he wastes away like something rotten,
like a garment eaten by moths.

fields.title: Job 14
fields.body_html:
A short life, full of trouble

A human being, born of a woman,
lives few days, and those days are full of trouble.
They spring up like a flower and wither;
they slip away like a shadow and do not last.
Do you really fix your eyes on such a one?
Will you bring me to trial before you?
Who can bring what is clean out of what is unclean?
No one!
Since their days are fixed,
and the number of their months is in your hands,
since you have set limits that they cannot cross,
then look away from them and let them rest,
until, like a hired worker, they finish their day.
For a tree there is hope:
if it is cut down, it will sprout again,
and its new shoots will not fail.
Even if its root grows old in the ground
and its stump dies in the dust,
at the first scent of water it will bud
and put out shoots like a young plant.
But a mortal dies and lies powerless;
a human being breathes their last, and where are they?
As water vanishes from a lake
and a river dries up and is parched,
so a person lies down and does not rise again;
until the heavens are gone, the dead will not awake
or be roused from their sleep.
If only you would hide me in Sheol
and keep me out of sight until your anger has passed,
then set a time for me and remember me!
If a mortal dies, will they live again?
All the days of my hard service I would wait
until my release came.
You would call, and I would answer you;
you would long for the creature your hands have made.
Then you would count my steps
but would not keep watch over my sin.
My offenses would be sealed up in a bag,
and you would cover over my guilt.
But as a mountain falls and crumbles away,
and a rock is moved from its place,
as water wears away stones
and floods wash away the soil of the land,
so you destroy the hope of mortals.
You overpower them once for all, and they are gone;
you change their face in death and send them away.
Their children may rise to honor, but they never know it;
their children may sink low, but they do not see it.
They feel only the pain of their own body;
they mourn only for themselves.

fields.title: Job 15
fields.body_html:
Eliphaz answers: windy words and a guilty mouth

Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
Should a wise person answer with windy knowledge
and fill his belly with the east wind?
Should he argue with useless talk,
with words that do no good?
But you are doing away with the fear of God
and hindering devotion before him.
For your guilt instructs your mouth,
and you choose the language of the crafty.
Your own mouth condemns you, not I;
your own lips testify against you.
Were you the first human being ever born?
Were you brought forth before the hills?
Do you listen in on God’s council?
Do you keep wisdom all to yourself?
What do you know that we do not know?
What do you understand that we do not?
Both the gray-haired and the aged are on our side,
people older than your father.
Are God’s comforts too small for you,
or a word spoken gently to you?
Why does your heart carry you away,
and why do your eyes flash,
so that you turn your anger against God
and let such words come out of your mouth?
How can a mortal be pure?
How can one born of a woman be righteous?
If God does not trust even his holy ones,
and the heavens are not pure in his sight,
how much less one who is vile and corrupt,
a person who drinks in wrongdoing like water!
Listen to me, and I will explain;
I will tell you what I have seen,
what the wise have declared
and have not hidden, what came from their ancestors,
to whom alone the land was given,
when no foreigner moved among them.
The wicked person writhes in pain all his days,
through all the years laid up for the ruthless.
Sounds of terror fill his ears;
when all is well, a destroyer attacks him.
He does not expect to escape from darkness;
he is marked out for the sword.
He wanders about for food, saying, ‘Where is it?’
He knows that the day of darkness is close at hand.
Distress and anguish fill him with terror;
they overpower him like a king ready for battle.
For he has stretched out his hand against God
and set himself up against the Almighty;
he charges at him defiantly,
with his thick, studded shield.
for he has covered his face with fat
and piled up fat on his waist,
and he has lived in ruined cities,
in houses no one should live in,
houses marked out to become heaps of rubble.
He will not stay rich, his wealth will not last,
and his possessions will not spread across the land.
He will not escape the darkness;
a flame will wither his young shoots,
and he will be swept away by the breath of God’s mouth.
Let him not deceive himself by trusting in what is empty,
for emptiness will be his reward.
It will be paid in full before his time,
and his branch will not flourish.
He will be like a vine that drops its grapes before they ripen,
like an olive tree that sheds its blossoms.
For the household of the godless will be barren,
and fire will consume the tents of those who take bribes.
They conceive trouble and give birth to wickedness;
their womb breeds deceit.

fields.title: Job 16
fields.body_html:
Comforters who bring trouble

Then Job answered:
I have heard many things like these;
you are all miserable comforters.
Will these windy words never end?
What is eating at you, that you keep answering?
I too could talk as you do,
if you were in my place;
I could string words together against you
and shake my head at you.
I would encourage you with my mouth,
and the comfort of my lips would ease your pain.
If I speak, my pain is not eased;
and if I keep silent, how much of it leaves me?
But now God has worn me out;
you have laid waste my whole household.
You have shriveled me up, and that has become a witness against me;
my gauntness rises up against me
and testifies to my face.
His anger has torn me, and he hounds me;
he grinds his teeth at me;
my enemy stabs at me with his eyes.
People gape at me with open mouths;
they strike my cheek in scorn;
they gang up together against me.
God hands me over to the unjust
and throws me into the clutches of the wicked.
I was at ease, but he shattered me;
he seized me by the neck and smashed me to pieces;
he set me up as his target.
His archers surround me.
Without mercy he slashes open my kidneys
and pours out my gall on the ground.
He breaks through me again and again, like a wall breached;
he charges at me like a warrior.
I have sewn sackcloth over my skin
and laid my strength in the dust.
My face is red with weeping,
and deep shadows lie on my eyelids.
even though my hands have done no violence
and my prayer is pure.
Earth, do not cover my blood;
let my cry find no place to rest.
Even now my witness is in heaven;
the one who vouches for me is on high.
My friends scorn me;
my eyes pour out tears to God.
that he would plead for a man with God,
as one pleads for a friend.
For only a few years will come
before I go the way of no return.

fields.title: Job 17
fields.body_html:
My spirit is broken, my days are snuffed out

My spirit is broken, my days are snuffed out;
the grave is waiting for me.
Surely mockers surround me,
and my eye must dwell on their taunts.
Please lay down a pledge for me; stand surety for me with yourself.
Who else will shake hands to back me?
For you have closed their minds to understanding;
therefore you will not let them triumph.
Whoever betrays friends for a share of the spoil,
the eyes of that person’s children will fail.
He has made me a byword among the peoples,
someone people spit on in the face.
My eye has grown dim with grief,
and my whole body is like a shadow.
Upright people are appalled at this,
and the innocent are stirred up against the godless.
The righteous hold to their way,
and those with clean hands grow stronger and stronger.
But come on, all of you, try again;
I will not find a wise person among you.
My days are over; my plans are torn apart,
the longings of my heart.
They turn night into day:
“Light is near,” they say, in the face of darkness.
If I look for Sheol as my home,
if I spread out my bed in the dark,
if I say to the pit, “You are my father,”
and to the worm, “My mother and my sister,”
Where then is my hope?
Who can see any hope for me?
Will my hope go down to the gates of Sheol?
Shall we sink into the dust together?

fields.title: Job 18
fields.body_html:
Bildad: the light of the wicked goes out

Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
How long before you all put an end to words?
Think it through, and then we can talk.
Why are we regarded as cattle,
as stupid in your sight?
You who tear yourself apart in your anger,
should the earth be abandoned for your sake,
or the rock be moved from its place?
Yes, the light of the wicked goes out;
the flame of his fire does not shine.
The light in his tent grows dark,
and the lamp above him goes out.
His strong stride is cut short,
and his own schemes bring him down.
For his own feet lead him into a net,
and he wanders onto a covered pit.
A trap grabs him by the heel;
a snare holds him tight.
A noose is hidden for him on the ground,
a trap lies in his path.
Terrors frighten him on every side
and dog his every step.
His strength is starved,
and disaster stands ready for him to stumble.
Disease eats away his skin;
the firstborn of death devours his limbs.
He is torn from the tent where he felt safe
and marched off to the king of terrors.
Nothing of his remains in his tent;
burning sulfur is scattered over his home.
His roots dry up below,
and his branches wither above.
All memory of him perishes from the land;
no one in the street speaks his name.
He is driven from light into darkness
and chased out of the world.
He has no children or grandchildren among his people,
no survivor where he once lived.
People of the west are appalled at his fate,
and people of the east are seized with horror.
Surely this is what becomes of the homes of the unjust,
the place of one who does not know God.

fields.title: Job 19
fields.body_html:
Job: it is God who has wronged me

Then Job answered:
How long will you torment me
and crush me with your words?
Ten times now you have insulted me;
you wrong me without shame.
Even if it is true that I have gone astray,
my error is my own concern.
If you really want to set yourselves above me
and use my disgrace as an argument against me,
then know that it is God who has wronged me
and thrown his net around me.
I cry out, “Violence!” but I get no answer;
I call for help, but there is no justice.
He has walled up my road so that I cannot get through;
he has covered my paths with darkness.
He has stripped me of my honor
and taken the crown from my head.
He tears me down on every side, and I am finished;
he has pulled up my hope like a tree.
His anger burns against me;
he counts me among his enemies.
His troops advance together;
they build up a siege ramp against me
and camp all around my tent.
He has driven my brothers far from me;
those who knew me have become strangers to me.
My relatives have let me down;
my close friends have forgotten me.
My household guests and my female servants treat me as a stranger;
I have become a foreigner in their eyes.
I call my servant, but he does not answer,
though I plead with him with my own mouth.
My breath is offensive to my wife;
I am loathsome to my own brothers.
Even young children despise me;
when I get up, they mock me.
All my closest friends detest me;
those I love have turned against me.
My bones stick to my skin and flesh;
I have escaped with only the skin of my teeth.
Have pity on me, have pity on me, you my friends,
for the hand of God has struck me.
Why do you hound me as God does?
Will you never have enough of my flesh?
Oh, that my words were written down,
that they were inscribed on a scroll,
with an iron chisel and with lead,
carved in the rock forever!
But I know that my Redeemer lives,
and that at the last he will stand upon the dust.
And after my skin has been destroyed like this,
yet in my flesh I will see God,
whom I myself will see on my side,
whom my own eyes will behold, and not as a stranger.
My heart faints within me!
If you say, “How we will hound him!”
and that the root of the trouble lies in me,
be afraid of the sword yourselves,
for wrath brings the punishment of the sword,
so that you may know that there is judgment.

fields.title: Job 20
fields.body_html:
The joy of the godless lasts only a moment

Then Zophar the Naamathite answered:
So my troubled thoughts urge me to reply,
because I am deeply stirred.
I have heard a rebuke that insults me,
and out of my understanding my spirit gives me a reply.
Surely you know how it has been from of old,
ever since humans were placed on the earth,
that the triumph of the wicked is brief,
and the joy of the godless lasts only a moment.
Though their pride rises up to the heavens
and their heads touch the clouds,
they will perish forever like their own dung;
those who used to see them will ask, “Where are they?”
They will fly away like a dream and not be found;
they will be driven off like a vision in the night.
The eye that once saw them will not see them again;
their place will look on them no more.
Their children will have to make amends to the poor;
their own hands must give back their wealth.
Their bones were full of youthful strength,
but it will lie down with them in the dust.
Though evil tastes sweet in their mouth
and they hide it under their tongue,
though they cannot bear to let it go
but keep it in their mouth,
their food turns sour in their stomach;
it becomes the venom of cobras inside them.
They swallow riches but vomit them up again;
God makes their stomach throw them out.
They suck the poison of cobras;
the viper’s fangs will kill them.
They will never enjoy the streams,
the rivers flowing with honey and cream.
They must give back what they toiled for and cannot swallow it;
they get no joy from the profits of their trading.
For they crushed the poor and left them destitute;
they seized houses they had not built.
Because their greed was never satisfied,
they will not save any of the things they prized.
Nothing was left after they had eaten;
therefore their prosperity will not last.
At the height of their plenty, distress will overtake them;
every hand of the wretched will turn against them.
When they are about to fill their stomach,
God will send his burning anger against them
and rain it down on them as their food.
They may run from an iron weapon,
but an arrow from a bronze bow will pierce them.
It is pulled out and comes out of their back,
the gleaming point out of their gall;
terrors come over them.
Total darkness is stored up for their treasures.
A fire no one fanned will consume them,
and anyone left in their tent will come to harm.
The heavens will expose their guilt,
and the earth will rise up against them.
The wealth of their house will be carried away,
swept off like floodwaters on the day of God’s anger.
This is what God gives to the wicked,
the heritage God has appointed for them.

fields.title: Job 21
fields.body_html:
Why do the wicked live?

Then Job answered:
Listen carefully to what I say,
and let that be the comfort you give me.
Bear with me while I speak;
then, when I have finished, go on mocking.
As for me, is my complaint against a human being?
Why then should I not be impatient?
Look at me and be appalled;
put your hand over your mouth.
When I think about it, I am terrified,
and my whole body shudders.
Why do the wicked go on living,
growing old and growing ever more powerful?
Their children are settled securely around them;
their descendants grow up before their eyes.
Their homes are safe and free from fear;
the rod of God does not strike them.
Their bulls breed without fail;
their cows calve and never miscarry.
They let their little ones run out like a flock of lambs,
and their children skip about.
They sing to the tambourine and the lyre
and make merry at the sound of the flute.
They live out their days in prosperity
and go down to Sheol in an instant.
Yet they say to God, “Leave us alone!
We have no wish to know your ways.
Who is the Almighty, that we should serve him?
What good will it do us to pray to him?”
Yet their prosperity is not in their own hands.
The advice of the wicked is far from me.
How often is the lamp of the wicked snuffed out?
How often does disaster fall on them,
or God deal out sorrows in his anger?
How often are they like straw before the wind,
like chaff swept away by a storm?
You say, “God stores up their punishment for their children.”
Let God repay the wicked themselves, so that they feel it!
Let them see their own ruin with their own eyes;
let them drink the wrath of the Almighty.
For what do they care about their family after they are gone,
when the number of their months has run out?
Can anyone teach God knowledge,
when he judges even those on high?
One person dies in full vigor,
completely secure and at ease.
Their pails are full of milk,
and their bones are rich with marrow.
Another dies in bitterness of soul,
never having tasted anything good.
They lie down alike in the dust,
and worms cover them both.
Look, I know what you are thinking,
the schemes you plot to wrong me.
For you say, “Where now is the prince’s house?
Where are the tents where the wicked lived?”
Have you never asked people who travel the roads?
Do you not accept what they report?
that the evil are spared on the day of disaster
and led to safety on the day of wrath.
Who confronts them to their face about the way they live?
Who pays them back for what they have done?
They are carried in procession to the grave,
and a watch is kept over their tomb.
The soil of the valley lies gently on them;
everyone walks behind in the procession,
and countless people go ahead.
So how can you comfort me with empty words?
Nothing is left of your answers but falsehood.

fields.title: Job 22
fields.body_html:
Eliphaz: is not your evil great?

Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered:
Can a person be of any use to God?
Even the wise benefit only themselves.
Is the Almighty pleased if you are righteous?
Is it any gain to him that you keep your ways blameless?
Is it because you revere him that he rebukes you
and enters into judgment with you?
Is your evil not great?
Is there no end to your iniquities?
You took pledges from your relatives for no reason
and stripped the poor of their clothing.
You did not give the weary water to drink,
and you kept back bread from the hungry.
The land belonged to the man with power,
and the favored man lived on it.
Widows you sent away with empty hands,
and the strength of the fatherless was crushed.
So now traps surround you on every side,
and sudden terror shakes you,
or darkness, where you cannot see,
and a flood of waters covers you.
Is not God up in the height of heaven?
See the topmost stars, how high they are!
And you ask, ‘What does God know?
Can he judge through the thick cloud?
Clouds are a screen around him, and he does not see;
he walks about on the dome of the sky.’
Will you hold to the ancient path
that wicked people have walked,
who were seized before their time,
whose foundations a river swept away?
They told God, ‘Keep away from us!
What can the Almighty do to us?’
And yet he had filled their houses with good things!
But the counsel of the wicked is far from me.
The righteous see it and are glad;
the innocent laugh at them:
Surely our enemies are destroyed,
and fire has eaten up what they left!
Come to terms with God and be at peace;
through this, good will come to you.
Take the teaching that comes from his mouth,
and set his words in your heart.
If you return to the Almighty, you will be built up again;
if you put wrongdoing far from your tent,
if you lay your gold in the dust,
your gold of Ophir among the stones of the streambeds,
then the Almighty will be your gold
and your silver piled high.
For then the Almighty will be your delight,
and you will raise your face to God.
You will pray to him, and he will listen to you,
and you will pay what you vowed.
Whatever you resolve will stand firm for you,
and light will shine along your paths.
When others are laid low, you will say, ‘Up!’
and he will save the humble.
He will set free even someone who is not innocent;
that one will go free because your hands are clean.

fields.title: Job 23
fields.body_html:
Job: if only I knew where to find him

Then Job answered:
Even today my complaint is defiant;
the hand on me weighs heavier than my groaning.
If only I knew how to find him,
how to come to his seat!
I would lay out my case before him,
and my mouth would be full of arguments.
I would learn what he would answer me
and understand what he would say to me.
Would he use his great power to argue against me?
No, he would surely pay attention to me.
There an upright person could reason with him,
and I would be set free by my judge forever.
I go to the east, and he is not there,
to the west, and I cannot make him out;
in the north, where he is at work, I do not see him;
he turns to the south, and I have no sight of him.
Yet he knows the road I am on;
when he has tried me, I will come out like gold.
My foot has held to his footsteps;
I have kept his way and not turned away from it.
From what his lips commanded I have not turned back;
I have stored up the words of his mouth above the food I live on.
But he is of one mind, and who can turn him back?
Whatever he desires, he does.
For he will carry out what he has decreed for me,
and he has many more decrees like it.
So I am terrified in his presence;
when I consider, I dread him.
God has weakened my heart;
the Almighty has filled me with terror.
Yet it is not darkness that has silenced me,
nor the deep gloom that covers my face.

fields.title: Job 24
fields.body_html:
Why does the Almighty not set times for judgment?

Why does the Almighty not set times for judgment?
Why do those who know him never see his days?
People move boundary stones;
they steal flocks and graze them as their own.
They drive off the orphan’s donkey;
they take the widow’s ox as security for a debt.
They push the needy off the road;
the poor of the land are all forced into hiding.
Look, like wild donkeys in the wilderness
the poor go out to their work, searching for food;
the desert gives them bread for their children.
They reap fodder in a field that belongs to another,
and they glean the vineyard of the wicked.
They spend the night naked, with no clothing,
and have nothing to cover them in the cold.
They are soaked by the mountain storms,
and having no shelter they hug the rocks.
Others snatch the fatherless child from the breast
and take pledges from the poor.
They go about naked, without clothing,
and they carry the sheaves while they go hungry.
Among the rows of olive trees they press out oil;
they tread the winepresses, yet they go thirsty.
In the city the dying groan,
and the wounded cry out for help;
yet God pays no attention to the wrong.
There are those who rebel against the light;
they do not know its ways
or stay on its paths.
Before daylight the murderer rises;
he kills the poor and the needy,
and at night he is like a thief.
The adulterer’s eye watches for the dusk; he says, “No eye will see me,”
and he covers his face.
In the dark they break into houses;
by day they shut themselves away;
they want nothing to do with the light.
For to all of them, morning is deep darkness;
they are at home with the terrors of the dark.
They are swept away swiftly on the face of the waters;
their share of the land is cursed;
no one turns toward their vineyards.
As drought and heat carry off the melted snow,
so Sheol carries off those who have sinned.
The womb that bore them forgets them; the maggot feasts on them;
they are remembered no more,
and wickedness is broken like a tree.
They prey on the childless woman
and do no good to the widow.
But God drags off the mighty by his power;
when he rises up, they have no assurance of life.
God may let them rest secure, and they rely on it,
but his eyes are on their ways.
They are exalted for a little while, and then they are gone;
they are brought low and gathered up like everyone else;
they are cut off like heads of grain.
If it is not so, who can prove me a liar
and show that my words are worth nothing?

fields.title: Job 25
fields.body_html:
How can a mortal be righteous before God?

Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:
Rule and dread belong to God;
he makes peace in his high places.
Can his armies be counted?
On whom does his light not rise?
How then can a mortal be righteous before God?
How can one born of a woman be pure?
Look, even the moon is not bright,
and the stars are not pure in his sight;
How much less a mortal, who is a maggot,
a human being, who is a worm!

fields.title: Job 26
fields.body_html:
How you have helped the powerless!

Then Job answered:
How you have helped the powerless!
How you have saved the arm that has no strength!
How you have advised one who lacks wisdom,
and shown such a wealth of insight!
With whose help have you uttered these words?
Whose spirit has spoken through you?
The spirits of the dead tremble,
those beneath the waters and all who live there.
Sheol lies naked before him;
Abaddon has no covering.
He stretches out the northern sky over empty space;
he hangs the earth on nothing.
He wraps up the waters in his clouds,
yet the clouds do not burst under their weight.
He veils the face of his throne,
spreading his cloud over it.
He has marked out a circle on the face of the waters
as a boundary between light and darkness.
The pillars of heaven tremble
and are stunned at his rebuke.
By his power he stirred up the sea;
by his skill he struck Rahab down.
By his breath the skies became clear;
his hand pierced the fleeing serpent.
Look, these are only the outer edges of his ways;
how faint the whisper we hear of him!
But the thunder of his power, who can understand it?

fields.title: Job 27
fields.body_html:
Job holds fast to his integrity

Job took up his discourse again and said:
As God lives, who has denied me justice,
and the Almighty, who has made my life bitter,
as long as I still have breath in me
and the breath of God is in my nostrils,
my lips will not speak what is wrong,
and my tongue will not utter lies.
Far be it from me to say that you are right;
until I die
I will not give up my integrity.
I hold on to my righteousness and will not let it go;
my conscience does not blame me
for any day of my life.
Let my enemy be like the wicked,
and my opponent like the unrighteous.
For what hope does the godless have when God cuts him off,
when he takes away his life?
Will God hear his cry
when trouble comes upon him?
Will he find delight in the Almighty?
Will he call on God at all times?
I will teach you about the power of God;
what the Almighty has in mind
I will not hide.
Look, all of you have seen it for yourselves;
why then do you talk such empty nonsense?
This is the portion a wicked person has from God,
the inheritance the ruthless receive from the Almighty:
If his children are many, they are destined for the sword,
and his descendants will never have enough to eat.
Those who survive him will be buried by the plague,
and his widows will not mourn.
Though he piles up silver like dust
and stores up clothes like heaps of clay,
he may store them up, but the righteous will wear them,
and the innocent will divide up the silver.
The house he builds is like a moth’s cocoon,
like a shelter put up by a watchman.
He lies down rich, but he will not be gathered to his ancestors;
he opens his eyes, and he is gone.
Terrors overtake him like a flood;
in the night a storm carries him off.
The east wind picks him up, and he is gone;
it sweeps him away from his place.
It hurls itself at him without mercy,
as he flees headlong from its power.
It claps its hands at him
and hisses at him from his place.

fields.title: Job 28
fields.body_html:
There is a mine for silver

There is a mine for silver
and a place where gold is refined.
Iron is taken from the earth,
and copper is smelted from ore.
Miners put an end to darkness;
they search to the farthest limits
for ore in gloom and deep darkness.
They cut a shaft far from where people live,
in places forgotten by those who walk above;
they hang and swing far from other people.
From the earth comes bread,
but underneath it is turned upside down as if by fire.
Its rocks are where sapphires are found,
and its dust contains gold.
No bird of prey knows that path;
the falcon’s eye has never seen it.
Proud beasts have not set foot on it;
the lion has never passed along it.
Miners put their hand to the flinty rock
and overturn mountains at their roots.
They cut tunnels through the rocks,
and their eyes see every treasure.
They dam up the trickling streams,
and bring hidden things out into the light.

But where can wisdom be found?

But where can wisdom be found?
Where is the place of understanding?
No human being knows its worth;
it is not found in the land of the living.
The deep says, “It is not in me,”
and the sea says, “It is not with me.”
It cannot be bought with the finest gold,
and its price cannot be weighed out in silver.
It cannot be weighed against the gold of Ophir,
against precious onyx or sapphire.
Gold and glass cannot equal it,
nor can it be traded for articles of fine gold.
Coral and crystal are not worth mentioning;
the price of wisdom is beyond rubies.
The topaz of Cush cannot equal it;
it cannot be weighed against pure gold.

God understands the way to wisdom

Then where does wisdom come from?
Where is the place of understanding?
It is hidden from the eyes of every living creature,
